“We’ve cut overhead costs with Lily Paper Service” 

says Joe Kronick, Director of Camp White Pine, Haliburton, Out. 


Two years ago Camp White Pine began its 
drive to create a cleaner, quieter, more 
economical kitchen and dining room opera¬ 
tion. The starting point was a switch to Lily 
Paper Service. Joe Kronick, Director of 
Camp White Pine hails the experiment as 
“an unqualified success”. “We’ve been able 
to cut down our kitchen and dining room 
staff by 10 people. Now, almost all our 
campers arc involved in table setting and 
service. Our kitchen is cleaner, our dining 
room is quieter, and our dishwashing 
machine handles our silverware and turns 
out a beautiful finished product. We’ve also 
licked hot water problems in the kitchen and 


showers—all because of Paper Service.” 
There’s a complete range of Lily paper cups 
and plates to make your camp operation 
easier. These light-weight, economical Lily 
products mean an end to tedious dish¬ 
washing . . . save valuable space, time and 
effort. The Lily range includes uncoatcd 
extra heavy weight, as well as plastic coated, 
non-absorbent plates that can’t soak up 
gravies or moist foods. 

Lily Paper Service is a safeguard against 
cross-contamination . . . removes the danger 
of broken glass and china. Enjoy a carefree 
camping operation this summer with Lily.

Helping Campers to Find . . . 

SPIRITUAL 

VALUES 


by Mary Purdy 

Toronto Y.W.C.A. Camp Tapawingo 

vvv/// 

//A\v 

This article is based on a talk given by Miss 
Purdy at the Ontario Camping Association 
Conference last year. 


Albert Schweitzer once said “The 
most important years in life are those 
between nine and fourteen. This is the 
time to plant the seeds of knowledge 
and character — afterward, it is too 
late. This is the time to acquaint the 
young with the great spiritual values 
of mankind.” 

If we attempt to analyse a child’s 
spiritual potential we realize that it is 
involved with his relations with other 
persons or with nature. Camp is the 
ideal setting for those long, long 
thoughts of youth which can give a 
youngster a sense of the Reality call it 
God, call it Truth or what you will, 
that must under-gird our material life. 
If modem culture has weakened the 
bases of faith, then the closeness to 


nature at camp, the chance for re¬ 
flection, the intimate association with 
people who believe in the primacy of 
things of the Spirit should aid in.the 
discovery, or re-discovery of faith. ’ 

I do not think that children are sent 
to camp by their parents for the 
religious value the camping programme 
contains. Rather are they sent by their 
parents to have a good time, a happy 
time in a camp setting for a part of 
their holidays. How do we contribute 
to this happiness—what is it? Margaret 
Govan, Past President of the Ontario 
Camping Association in her article en¬ 
titled “The Happy Camper” (CAN¬ 
ADIAN CAMPING, June, 1961) ob¬ 
served, “the camper who is a happy 
child by nature, will be happy as a 
king in most of our camps. The trouble 
is that many of our children are not 
naturally happy. How could they be? 
They have a strange nursery ... a 
world of tension, fear, trouble and 
struggle; a man-made, materialistic 
world where even the child consumer 
is being battered on every side, to 
consume more and so become less self- 
sufficient and self-reliant; a world of 
values which cut across other values; a 
world of change and upset, unpredict¬ 
able, without roots! And our children 
reflect the world. They bring to camp 
what Fritz Redl calls ‘shadows from 
home’—worries, tensions, fears, aggres¬ 
siveness, hostility, prejudice, and values 
which are anti-social, unethical, even 
immoral.” 

These campers need to have a good 
happy time, they need a sense of 
achievement as they master new skills, 
but primarily, they need a sense of 
values, a measuring stick. Children 
need roots—or a sense of being rooted 
in something. Perhaps this is the main 
contribution a camp can make to the 
life of a child—to give him a sense of 
belonging to some stable immovable 
thing. 


44 


Canadian Camping 


Religion, to my mind, is the business 
of the church. My job as a camp 
director is to try to put the church’s 
teachings into action in a camp setting. 
I know that church camps will have a 
different point of view on this, and 
rightly so, because their focus is a 
different one. Church camps are geared 
to continue the religious instruction 
being given in their own particular 
denomination, but most of us are not 
equipped to do this. 

You may remember that in this 
magazine’s “Sermons Under the Sun” 
I once said, “The best sermon under 
the sun is one that is not ‘preached’. 
Children do not like to be ‘preached 
at’. Rather, do they like to share 
some thought of yours—or better still, 
to share some thought of theirs with 
you. It has been my experience that a 
small thought with a large meaning 
can best be grasped and understood by 
young persons. The thought they grasp 
immediately, the larger meaning behind 
the thought grows and develops with 
the child!* 

God has created a new day, 

Silver and green and gold. 

Live that the sunset may find us 
Worthy His gift to hold. 

These four lines even the youngest 
child can understand: just for today, 
I have to be kind, love my neighbors, 
be lovely, do no ugly or mean thing. 
One day is an easy span of time for 
children to comprehend. Later, those 
same children will realize that such 
attitudes practised one day at a time 
have become their patterns of behaviour 
for all time. 

Children like little poems. Thoughts 
in rhyme tend to linger longer in their 
minds: 

Let me be a little kinder, 

Let me be a little blinder 

To the faults of those around me. 


or 

I have to live with myself, and so 

I have to be fit for myself to know. 

I don’t want to keep on a closet shelf 

A lot of secrets about myself. 
or 

God who touchest earth with beauty, 

Make me lovely too. 

The best sermon under the sun, very 
often, is the thought we share with 
each other at flag-raising—as we begin, 
together, a new day all silver and green 
and gold. We sit on the rocks at our 
camp each morning, watching the sun 
creep up over the hill, over the tree tops 
and, finally, over the dining hall roof. 
We listen to the slap of the water on 
the shore behind us. We see and hear a 
new day dawning. We know that we 
have a fresh, new shiny day in which 
to be a little kinder, a little blinder to 
others faults, a little more lovely than 
yesterday. It really matters little that 
we cannot hear all the words of the 
poem or story being read to us this 
morning. We are sharing something 
very lovely with each other — the 
dawning of a new, silver and green 
and gold start. 

Every child and every staff member 
has some precious thought to share 
with you and the rest of the camp. 
Encourage this sharing. Have plenty of 
reference material easily accessible to 
those planning the thought for the day 
or for the Sunday Chapel service. Let 
them talk to you. Don’t you do all the 
talking at them. Because you see, the 
little shared thoughts with homely 
meanings are the best sermons under 
the sun. 

A man named Edwards once wrote 
“If you would have your child be 
something in the world, teach him to 
depend on himself. Let him learn that 
it is by close and strenuous personal 
application he must rise—that he must, 
in short, make himself and be the 

turn to page 68 


Toronto, Canada , February 1963 


45 



A New Feature 


The Challenge 
of Camping 


THE 

VICE-PRESIDENTS’ 

PAGE 


by Grant McKeen, 

Vice President CCA , Alberta 
Director, Camp Keewaydwin 


What is it that makes camping such 
a worthwhile experience? Is it the 
spiritual values in the camp? Is it the 
fun? Is it the outdoor living? Is it the 
doing and learning? 

There are young people today who 
are willing to settle for low success 
rather than risk high failure. The 
average youth, it seems, would rather 
work for a large corporation than start 
his own company; he seeks security in 
the corporation rather than face the 
“challenge” of the outside world. Can 
we do something about this in camp¬ 
ing? I believe we do when we offer 
enough adventure and challenge which 
he can learn to meet and overcome. In 
this way we equip him better for the 
wider challenges ahead. 

Consider the special features of 
camping: fun, happiness, character 
development, personal growth, adven¬ 
ture. These give a boy security; they 
put hope and meaning into life for 
him. The mere fact he is away from 
home helps start him on the road to 
independence and self-reliance. To our 
older children, however, the word 
“future” generally means a loosely 
wrapped bundle of worries. Not so 
their future while at camp. Here a 
youth will see and have opportunities 
to overcome his worries. He discovers 
that the individual is very important to 


the total camp as an individual, and 
that everyone is trying to help him to 
succeed. In our camp programmes we 
face him with reality in the challenges 
of adventure, friendship, character 
development, in learning about nature. 
These are necessary features of life at 
camp — we try to help our youth 
respond to them. 

Where in our busy world and society 
today does our youth feel at ease other 
than at camp? Here he lives in a 
world where character not competition 
is important. Here a child can think, 
understand, learn interesting skills, 
appreciate the spiritual harmony that 
comes from living close to nature. 

I am sure that camping will play one 
of the largest roles in the future outdoor 
education and recreation of youth. Are 
we aware of the needs of our future 
campers? Let us consider those I have 
suggested and then give our campers 
the experience that will help them to 
meet challenges, and in so doing we 
will also make our nation stronger both 
spiritually and physically. 

May I add that when we fail to 
live up to our philosophy of camping, 
we must still keep on trying and look 
to God for guidance. 


46 


Canadian Camping 



The Quebec Camp 

for Diabetic Children 


by Walter D. Mingie, B.Sc., 
Camp Director 


The Quebec Camp for Diabetic 
Children operated Camp Carowanis for 
two periods of three weeks each during 
the summer of 1962, and accommo¬ 
dated sixty boys and girls in each 
period, aged from eight to fifteen years. 
Camp Carowanis is situated sixty miles 
north-east of Montreal, three miles 
from the town of Ste. Agathe in the 
Laurentian Mountains. We are for¬ 
tunate in having an isolated site whose 
closest neighbour is half a mile down 
the lake and hidden from view. 

A camp especially for diabetic boys 
and girls is necessary because regular 
camps are not equipped to look after 
these children. Because we feel that a 
camping experience is worth while, 
there has to be a camp geared to take 
care of these children’s needs. Also, 
the camp situation is ideal for teaching 
the children to live with diabetes. Al¬ 
though we have a course of instruc¬ 
tional talks on diabetes by the doctors 
and dietitians in both French and 
English, we try to de-emphasize the 
special routines and to accentuate the 
normal camping activities. 

We play softball, soccer and volley¬ 
ball. We have regattas, treasure hunts, 
campfires, picnics, canoe trips, square¬ 
dancing and Saturday night plays. We 
teach the campers handicrafts and 
canoeing. We also teach them to test 
their own urine and to administer their 
own insulin. And I hope we teach 
them that by carefully following their 
diets, they can lead healthy normal lives. 


You would find us different from 
other camps, of course, firstly because 
before breakfast every morning all the 
campers report to the camp infirmary. 
Here several counsellors, two doctors 
and two nurses are on duty to supervise 
and to teach the campers to give their 
own insulin. At this time, also, each 
camper is given a glass of fruit juice. 

We are different, secondly, because 
at meal time there are no “seconds” 
even in bread and butter. Each camper 
has a wholesome diet to suit his or her 
needs written on a diet card. After 
grace the campers, a table group at a 
time, file into the kitchen where our 
two dietitians serve the meal to each 
individual. The name of each camper 
is marked on the table at his place. 
Therefore, it is an easy job for each 
camper’s milk, bread, butter, and des¬ 
sert to be put on the table ahead 
of time. 

We are different, thirdly, because we 
provide mid-morning, mid-afternoon 
and evening snacks for our campers 
and counsellors. The mid-morning 
snack is generally fruit. In the after¬ 
noon it is milk and cookies, and before 
bedtime it is generally biscuits, or bread 
and jam, with a cup of milk. Cheese 
and crackers are brought around to the 
tents and cabins after the campers are 
in bed. 

Fourthly, we are different because we 
run an afternoon programme starting 
ten minutes after lunch. Then, when 
the campers are in need of a rest, we 
have the traditional quiet hour in mid¬ 
afternoon followed by the afternoon 
swim. 

turn to page 63 


Toronto , Canada , February 1963

TOILETS 


for use in 

Summer Cumps 


by S. C. Cowan, C.S.I.(C), Eng. Tech., 
Environmental Sanitation Branch , 
Ontario Department of Health 


Most persons, whether adults or 
children, attending summer camps are 
from the urban areas of our country, 
and enjoy spending their vacations in 
surroundings which are different. It 
naturally follows that most summer 
camps are usually located far from 
cities and towns and are not equipped 
with municipal facilities such as water 
supply and sewage disposal systems. 
Each camp therefore must be con¬ 
sidered as a small but complete munici¬ 
pality having the usual problems 
associated with water supply and sew¬ 
age disposal. 

When considering toilets in summer 
camps, one must not only consider 
convenience but must insure that the 
method of waste disposal is such that 
the health of those at the camp and 
the health of others in the area is not 
endangered. Ground and surface waters 
which may be the source of water 
supply for other people must not be 
contaminated. 

Regardless of the type of toilet to be 
installed, certain criteria should be 
applied to all—the provision of separate 
facilities for each sex and for camp 
staff, urinals for boys’ camps, hand¬ 
washing facilities, adequate screening 
for fly control, be convenient for use 
but affording the necessary degree of 
privacy, be adequately illuminated and 


inspected daily so that maintenance is 
of the highest order. In this respect, 
the seats should be scrubbed with a 
detergent solution at least once daily 
or oftener as needed. 

The choice of toilet facilities to be 
provided will be determined by finan¬ 
cial considerations, the availability of 
water and the type of terrain. 

Water carriage systems, which con¬ 
sist of a regular or modified water closet 
connected to a septic tank and tile bed, 
are becoming increasingly popular in 
summer camps as a method of sewage 
disposal. The septic tank system con¬ 
sists essentially of a septic tank which 
partially treats the sewage and the field 
tile bed which distributes the liquid 
effluent to the soil. 

The septic tank’s purpose is to settle 
out and break down by bacterial action 
some of the waste solids which cannot 
be absorbed by the soil in the field 
tile bed. It is important that the tank 
be large enough to provide the required 
amount of settling time. The septic 
tank does not eliminate odours or des¬ 
troy all solid matter. Some suspended 
solids and dissolved solids are carried 
over into the tile bed. However, this 
putrescible material is broken down 
further by bacteria in the soil. 

The field tile bed consists of per¬ 
forated pipes or short lengths of tile. 


48 


Canadian Camping 


laid with open joints in trenches so 
that the effluent can escape through the 
joints and be absorbed by the surround¬ 
ing soil. The size of the subsurface 
disposal bed is directly determined by 
the percolation rate of the soil. It is 
emphasized that sewage is not purified 
in the septic tank. The liquid effluent 
leaving the tank is as highly polluted 
as the wastes entering the tank. That 
is why it is extremely important that 
the effluent does not pollute the ground 
water table or a water course which 
may be used for water supplies. 

Some areas are unsuitable for sewage 
disposal by means of regular septic 
tanks and field tile beds in conjunction 
with the usual water carriage system by 
reason of insufficient soil, high ground 
water table or insufficient water supply. 
In these areas, modifications of the 
regular septic tank and field tile bed 
are used, such as the modified auto¬ 
matic-flush type and the pail-a-day 
type. 

The modified automatic-flush type 
toilet generally is used where water is 
scarce or where insufficient area is 
available for the size of field tile bed 
required by a regular flush toilet system. 
The same criteria regarding soil depth 
and percolation rates should be used to 
determine the size of the tile bed 
required. 

The main difference between the 
modified flushing systems and the regu¬ 
lar flushing systems is the quantity of 
water used. The modified systems use 
approximately one quart of water at 
each flush and the tile bed should be 
designed on the basis of at least one 
gallon of water per person per day. 
In any case, the total length of tile 
should not be less than 40 feet for 
toilet flushing only. Where hand basins, 
kitchen wastes, and shower wastes are 
discharged to the same septic tank as 
the modified toilet, then the septic tank 
and tile bed should be of sufficient size 


to accommodate the increased sewage 
flow. 

The pail-a-day system is used where 
two gallons of water per seat can be 
added daily and where a subsurface 
leaching system is feasible. It consists 
of a water tight tank in which the water 
level is controlled by the position of the 
over-flow to ensure submergence of the 
end of the drop-pipe from the toilet 
seat fixture. Effluent from the overflow 
discharges into a tile bed laid in per¬ 
meable soil. The action in the tank is 
similar to that of a septic tank, and 
the tile bed should be designed in a 
similar manner to the modified auto¬ 
matic-flush system. 

Until recent years, the sanitary privy 
was the most common means of sewage 
disposal, both in camps and in most 
rural areas. Various types of privies 
have been and still are being used, 
such as the earth pit type, the pail 
type and the concrete vault type. 

Earth pit privies are recommended 
only where there is at least a seven foot 
depth of earth above the ground water 
table, rock or impervious clay layer. 
This is to permit the digging of a pit 
five feet below the original ground level 
while still retaining a minimum of two 
feet, (four feet is preferable), between 
the bottom of the pit and the upper 
surface of the ground water table. It 
is also important to locate the privy 
as far away from any well as possible 
but, in any case, not closer than 100 
feet. The privy should be located so 
that it is down-stream from the well in 
the direction of the flow of the ground 
water. This will usually mean that the 
privy is located where the ground sur¬ 
face is at a lower elevation than the 
ground surface at the well, since the 
slope of the ground water table usually 
follows that of the ground surface. 
However, this is not always the case 
and care must be taken in this regard. 

turn to page C5 


Toronto, Canada, February 1963 


49 


AMONG 

OURSELVES Mr, and Mrs, Van 



With commercialism making constant 
inroads into seemingly every field of 
professional endeavour, it is a happy 
observation to note that in our field of 
camping, there are still many who arc 
sincerely dedicated to camping as such 
—camping, first and foremost. 

Two such people are F. M. Van 
Wagner and his wife, Catherine. He is 
the Owner-Director of Camp Nominin- 
gue, a private boy’s camp situated on 
Little Lake Nominingue, high up in 
Quebec’s beautiful Laurentian Moun¬ 
tains—about 125 miles from Montreal. 

Mr. and Mrs. Van, as they have 
been for years aff ectionately referred to 
by campers and counsellors, met at 
McGill University in 1921 ; interestingly 
enough, she as the student and he as 
the teacher. From the outset, it was 
quite obvious that they shared a true 
interest, understanding and love for the 
“out-of-doors”, and shortly after they 
were married. 

Van took his degree in Physical Edu¬ 
cation at Springfield University in 1917 
and received his diploma at McGill in 


by G. H. Merrill, 

Director, Camp Nominingue 


1925. He was Director of the Y.M.C.A. 
camp from 1920 until 1924. 

In the fall of 1924, Van and a 
McGill associate of his. Hay Finlay, 
decided that they would operate their 
own camp a camp wherein they could 
enunciate the many personal ideas they 
shared regarding camping. 

They were assisted by the C.P.R. in 
locating a site, which at that time, 
could be expressed only as a barren 
wilderness. It is to their great credit 
that out of this seemingly lost world, 
they carved out what is today, one of 
the finest camping sites in the country. 
To describe Van’s considerable efforts 
and toil would usurp too much time 
and space to remain within the scope 
of this article. Suffice it to say, it was 
a task which men of lesser quality 
would not have undertaken. 





50 


Canadian Camping 



The summer of 1925 saw Gamp 
Nominingue begin its first season with 
an overall enrolment of twelve campers 
—a far cry from the 270 boys who spent 
the summer of 1962 at camp. Little, 
perhaps, did Van and Catherine realize 
in 1925 that thirty-seven years later, 
they would be running one of the 
largest private camps in Canada. 

Now, who are these two remarkable 
people? What is their true contribution 
to the Canadian camping movement? I 
think it can be stated without qualifica¬ 
tion that no two individuals have made 
any greater effort to promote the true 
spirit of camping outdoors than Van 
and Catherine. 

• Sincerity is a keynote in any pursuit, 
no matter what it may be. To pay lip- 
service to good intentions is not suffi¬ 
cient. There must be will, purpose and 
intent to the individual’s aim. To this 
end, Van and Catherine exemplify 
these all-important qualities. It is their 
unswerving feeling that a boy should 
learn to live in the natural setting, 
which, today so many of us avoid. 
They have always believed that canoe¬ 
tripping in nature’s wilderness, a night 
of sleep under the stars, cooking one’s 
meal over an outdoor fire, washing in 
the fresh waters of the lake—these and 
other natural experiences—are a neces¬ 
sary part of a boy’s growing up. They 
have set a course which has been un¬ 
alterable, and for which many campers, 
both past and present, will be forever 
grateful. 

Van and Catherine are not impract¬ 
ical people, for they well realize that 
running a large organization requires 
a great deal of practical thinking. They 
are also aware that the average youth 
of today is not initially looking for the 
type of experience which they are so 
anxious to promote. Nonetheless, it is 
quite apparent that after a boy has spent 
a season or two at Camp Nominingue, 
he becomes imbued with the true spirit 


of camping life as indicated by Van 
and Catherine. 

In this era of rush, rush, rush, it is 
a singular pleasure to observe the quite 
pleasant existence that Van and Cath¬ 
erine have made for themselves. From 
the first breath of spring until Decem¬ 
ber, they spend every weekend in the 
quiet, tranquil atmosphere of their 
Laurentian home. Catherine has, over 
the years, become both a lover of and 
authority on natural things, and there 
is no tree, plant, insect or animal of 
which she does not know something. 
The Nature Cabin, where she is cura¬ 
tor, is a fascinating centre—a place 
where, in the summer, small boys can 
always be found satisfying their natural 
and healthy curiosities. 

While Catherine employs much of 
her time pursuing the wonders of 
nature, Van is forever occupied with 
planning and making improvements on 
his campsite. It is to his considerable 
credit that he is never fully satisfied, 
and no matter how successful one 
season may have been, is always seeking 
ways of making the next season a better 
one. The keynote, however, is that the 
improvement is entirely directed with 
the campers in mind. What will give 
these boys a better and more healthy ex¬ 
perience? This is Van’s main concern. 

Van and Catherine have dedicated 
their lives to camping both in summer, 
and winter. Few men have attained*^ 
the stature in their chosen field as has 
Van. He is looked upon as one of the 
real camping authorities in Canada and 
the United States. Just recently, he 
has completed a highly successful term 
of office as President of the Canadian 
Camping Association. His work is 
never-ending. While there is breath in 
his body, he will pursue the course 
which has given such meaning to his 
life, which has opened up new vistas 

turn to page 69

A New Challenge to Canadian Youth 


THE DUKE OF EDINBURGH 
AWARD 


A Preliminary Report 
by Norm McKee 

Director, Camp Ki-Wa-Y, 

Kitchener-Waterloo Y.M.C.A. Camps 


Objective 

‘It is the belief of His Royal High¬ 
ness, Prince Philip, that there is a 
great wealth of excellence among 
young people, particularly among those 
leaving school at an early age, which 
is allowed to go undiscovered. This 
accounts in no small measure for the 
apathy and frustration which is in 
evidence, particularly in cities. He 
believes that all young people should be 
given the fullest opportunities to make 
the best use of their leisure both actively 
and creatively and that the note to 
strike in providing such opportunities 
is one of Challenge; the wider the 
challenge, the bigger the response. This 
is the main purpose of the award 
scheme.’ 

The above statement is the reason¬ 
ing which underlies a scheme of 
achievements and awards aimed at 
boys and girls in the age group 14-19. 
This scheme, as it has been applied in 
the United Kingdom, is known as the 
Duke of Edinburgh Award. It is a 
scheme designed to help the youth of 
to-day develop character, a sense of 
achievement, and individual initiative. 
In its present form the scheme is not 
designed as a separate programme, but 
as a means of strengthening and aug¬ 
menting existing activities for youth 
(e.g. Boy Scouts or Girl Guides work¬ 
ing for proficiency badges in the 


United Kingdom can qualify for recog¬ 
nition under the Duke of Edinburgh 
award scheme). 

The scheme divides itself into 4 areas 
of activities: 

Section A—Rescue and Public Service 
Training 

This calls for proficiency in one or 
more subjects, such as First Aid, Life 
Saving, Mountain Rescue Training, 
Civil Defence (E.M.O.) etc. 

Section B—Expeditions 

Expeditions are group enterprises in¬ 
volving from twenty-four hours in open 
country to three nights camping out 
in wild country. 

Section C—Pursuits and Projects 
These are creative activities calling 
for sustained effort rather than a 
specific standard of accomplishment, 
with the aim of developing natural 
interests and aptitudes of individuals. 
These subjects cover a wide field of 
which the following are examples: 

Arts: Collections (e.g. stamps, for¬ 
eign coins, match boxes, etc.) draw¬ 
ing, music, photography, etc. 
Craftmanship: Metal work wood¬ 
work, model making, mechanical, 
electrical, etc. 

Technical Skill: Gliding, sailing 
canoeing, rock climbing, judo, under¬ 
water diving (SCUBA), etc. 

Section D—Fitness: 

The attainment of established stan¬ 
dards in athletics and swimming, to^ 
gether with other activities calling for 
stamina, strength, skill, speed, etc.

opportunity for character growth be¬

ON LIVING 
WITH 

THE WINTER 
IN 

THE COUNTRY 

During the past twenty-five years 
most Canadians who do not ski have 
turned against the winter. They say 
they detest it, and I have often said 
the same myself. Like most of us, I 
had forgotten that winter is our truest 
season in this land. 

But one Sunday late in November 
my wife and I went down to the 
country, and the sense of the winter 
came back again ... On this day I 
forgot the H-bomb because suddenly I 
remembered that once upon a time I 
had been young enough to know what 
life in the winter can be like. 

These days that are overtures to 
winter in Canada are young days. The 
country looks new, its structure visible 
as it never is in summer. The lake 
seemed more like a well than a lake. 
Its centre was like a polished opal, 
drawing into its depths a pale sky, 
while along the shoreline against the 
rime on the rocks the water had the 
opaque gloss of ink. 

I said to my wife: “I’ve just realized 
something. I’ve lost my sense of the 
winter ... I used to know it pretty 
well.” 



by Hugh MacLennan 

Reprinted in part frotn SATURDAY 
NIGHT by kind permission of the author 
and the publisher. 


“So did I,” she said. 

“/ used to sleep out in it. I never 
told you that, did I?” 

Her face expressed surprise and she 
asked if we had a sleeping porch at¬ 
tached to our house. 

“No, I slept in a tent. As a matter of 
fact, between the ages of eleven and 
twenty-one, the only time I ever slept 
inside four walls was a week when I 
was sick.” 

“You mean, you slept in a tent in the 
winter?” 

“It didn’t seem a peculiar thing to do 
at the time. What does seem peculiar 
is that I’d forgotten all about it. I 
really had.” 

“What ever gave you the idea?” 

It happened like this. In the summer 
of my twelfth year I went to a boys’ 
camp in Nova Scotia where we slept on 
the bare ground under canvas. The 
mid-August day when the camp broke 
up and we came home happened to be 
very hot—the sticky heat you some¬ 
times get near the sea—and the soft 
bed in my parents’ house so smothered 
me that I could not sleep. 


54 


Canadian Camping 




The next day the temperature was 
nearly ninety and my father suggested 
that I sleep outside. He remembered a 
little tent in the basement he had used 
years ago when he went fishing, and 
suggested I get it out and pitch it in 
the back yard. 

In those days in Halifax the life was 
not much different from life in a 
village even though we had the harbor, 
the university, the hospitals, the 
Government House, the curfew gun on 
the Citadel and the memory of the ex¬ 
plosion which had smashed a third of 
the town a few years before. Behind 
every house was some sort of back yard 

— the word “yard” had probably 
reached us from New England Loyalists 

— and most of these had a kitchen 
garden, a few fruit trees and a one- 
horse stable which might or might not 
have been converted into a one-car 
garage. 

In the early 1920s there was still a 
faint smell of stable behind the houses 
and a reasonably strong smell of it in 
the streets. Each yard was separated 
from its neighbors by a rough board 
fence on the top of which prowling 
tomcats sat in the nights and howled at 
the female cats they knew were inside 
the houses. 

It was in a yard like this that I 
pitched my tent, installed a battered 
old hospital cot and a packing case to 
hold a saucer with a candle in it. The 
first night outside I slept dreamlessly 
and the next day I told my parents I 
intended to stay out until school began. 

When school did begin on the first of 
September it was still hot weather, so I 
told them I would stay out until it got 
cool. In the first week of October the 
mornings were cool enough, but there 
was dew on the ripe apples and pears 
and waking up in such air was a sensual 
experience as delicious as any I can 
remember. I told my parents I intended 
staying out until it got really cold. 


Three weeks later it began. I woke 
in stillness absolute, with every sense- 
perception alive. My nose was wet and 
cold, but the pillow side of my face was 
unnaturally warm. The tent was dark 
and heavy, its sides sagged in close to 
my cot, the ridge pole was bent and 
when I got up I saw a foot of snow on 
the ground. 

It was a new world that morning 
with the sun blazing over the back 
fence and tracks in the snow — one 
set of tracks coming to the tent and 
another going away from it. I realized 
that a tomcat had entered in the night, 
had slept for a while on the foot of my 
bed, and had gone away again. After 
breakfast that day I rode to school on 
the rear runner of a fishmonger’s sleigh 
wearing a pair of cowhide larrigans 
greasy with linseed oil. 

“It’s time you stopped this nonsense,” 
my father said that night at dinner. 
“Now you’ve had your snow, so come 
inside. Another snowfall and that tent 
will break. I bought it before the war 
and the canvas must be getting rotten.” 

I begged him to let me stay out until 
it became impossibly cold, and he 
shrugged his shoulders and said he 
supposed I could do what I liked. After 
all, he was a Scotch Calvinist and it 
had not occurred to him that living out 
in the winter can be a sensual exper¬ 
ience. He merely believed it was un¬ 
comfortable and assumed, without 
really thinking about it, that discomfort 
was somehow connected with virtue. 

It never did get impossibly cold, 
though it got so cold that today, in my 
middle age, I wonder what has hap¬ 
pened to my cells and metabolism 
since the time when I slept pleasantly 
in a below-zero atmosphere. The Can¬ 
adian climate in the early 1920s had a 
three to four degree lower mean 
average that it has now, and a tem¬ 
perature of twelve below in the moist 

I 


Toronto, Canada, February 1963 


55 



sea air of Nova Scotia feels colder than 
a temperature of thirty below on a 
windless day in Manitoba. 

One night in my first January the 
fibres of the fruit trees cracked in the 
frost like rifle shots, and when I came 
into the house the next morning and 
saw on the thermometer outside the 
kitchen window that it was sixteen be¬ 
low zero I felt more pleased .(why, I 
wonder?) than I did the first time I 
saw the title of a novel of mine on the 
best-seller list of The New York Times. 

I never used a sleeping bag. Army 
blankets, army socks, two pairs of flan¬ 
nel pajamas, a red beret and a hot 
water bottle which always became cold 
before dawn was all the equipment I 
needed. The only part of me that ever 
got cold—except on the night the old 
tent broke and dumped a load of snow 
on top of me — was my nose. And a 
cold nose when the rest of you is warm 
is a better sedative than a quarter-grain 
seconal. 

Stars were visible through the open 
end of the tent and so was moonlight 
washing the snow. Sometimes in a thaw 
I fell asleep to the regular drip of 
icicles, and on misty nights I heard the 
harbor bells and the groan of the fog¬ 
warning booming in from Chebucto 
Head. 

On the very cold nights phenomena 
belonging to the science of physics (or 
is it chemistry?) became high poetry. 
My breath made snow, real snow. Issu¬ 
ing warm from the lungs, it mounted to 
the ridgepole and turned into a cloud 
in the still, frigid air. When it con¬ 
gealed, it was converted into a delicate 
snow-mist which descended and settled 
lightly on the top blanket, and that was 
the subtlest sensation of all. 

The first time it happened I woke 
with an orange sun staring through the 
tent door and found myself warm under 


a quarter-inch covering of the softest, 
lightest snow I ever saw, each crystal 
distinct, and as the sunlight washed 
over it, for a few moments it was like 
lying under a rainbow. 

It was a queer way to live, I suppose 
and that may have been why I told 
none of my friends about it. The 
neighbors knew. They couldn’t help 
knowing, for I installed a small fire- 
gong inside the tent with a cord run- 
ining about twenty yards along 
pulleys to the house, where it entered 
the kitchen through a hole bored in 
the window frame. 

Our Newfoundland maid used to 
jerk the cord to wake me up when she 
came downstairs in the morning to set 
the fires and everyone in the neighbor¬ 
hood heard it. These days that fire-gong 
would have finished me — people 
would have protested about it to the 
police — but thirty-five years ago 
nearly everyone got up at the same 
time, which was between seven and 
seven-thirty, and at least one neighbor 
told my mother that the gong saved him 
the trouble of setting an alarm clock. 

The years passed, and I can’t re¬ 
member one from the other. I was 
sleeping in the tent through most of my 
education, and I stayed in it until the 
day before I sailed from Halifax to take 
up a Rhodes Scholarship in Oxford. 

This year a city-bred critic, reviewing 
my last book of essays in a London 
journal, complained he could find next 
to nothing in them because they, were 
the product of a personality so alien to 
his own that he could not comprehend 
it. To some degree the tent must have 
been responsible for this. I realize that 
it gave me such an acute awareness of 
climate that in most of my novels the 
weather is apt to develop into a 
character as important as the people.

CAMP 

CAP3RS 

THE TRAGIC DEMISE 
OF ESMERALDA 

One day when the camp looked as 
if it had been sprayed with papers, 
Esmeralda was born. She had arrived 
at camp (by report only) at dinner 
time that day. According to the story 
teller she really had been created one 
rainy day the previous summer by a 
cabin group all of whom were now 
present and wriggling with excitement 
over being part of a story. 

She was a life-size puppet who had 
come out of the craft shop and dropped 
papers when nobody was about, stuck 
tired-out chewing gum here and there, 
and left other people’s belongings in 
the oddest places! Nobody had 
dreamed of her future when she had 
been carried off to that cabin. Her 
career began when she was given a 
vitamin pill. Now she reappeared each 
year when it seemed necessary to point 
the moral. 

Last summer she had turned up quite 
early in the season. Wrapped caramels, 
it seems, have their drawbacks—or, for 
someone like Esmeralda, their come¬ 
back. The very next morning a tragic 
report was brought to the breakfast 
table. Esmeralda had been strung up 
on the flag pole! Somebody had noticed 
it on the way to breakfast. (We have 
flag-raising after breakfast since the 
dining-room and the flag pole are at 
opposite ends of camp.) The head of 
the swimming department and the 
nurse were excused to rescue her; one 
was to do ‘mouth-to-mouth’ resuscita¬ 
tion, and the other to render first aid. 
To no avail. Esmeralda was carried 
off to the infirmary, a sorry bundle of 
clothes and Kapoc. 

Who had perpetrated the dastardly 
deed? A senior cabin group who had 



What were some of the camp capers 
that happened at your camp over the years? 
The editorial committee would welcome 
contributions to this new series . 

dreams of becoming detectives, rose to 
the challenge. The trial will be long 
remembered for it was an amazing 
piece of creative dramatics a la Perry 
Mason. Four innocent counsellors were 
arraigned. (The true culprit, an ex¬ 
counsellor on a visit to camp, had 
departed.) The counsellors refused the 
kind offer of a defense lawyer, pre¬ 
ferring to speak for themselves. But it 
was useless. Evidence was piled up, 
irrelevant, contradictory, it didn’t mat¬ 
ter. The crowning piece was a perfect 
spate of French from a French- 
Canadian camper—all nonsense as was 
found out too late, but it wouldn’t have 
mattered in any case. The affidavit 
from the nurse was a masterly bit of 
prose overflowing with medical terms. 
All four defendants were condemned 
by a hanging jury. (The juniors rose 
in a body and objected, but they were 
turncoats who had been passing on 
rumours all day!) The defense lawyer 
recited, “The quality of mercy is not 
strained” etc. The judge pronounced 
the sentence: hard labour picking up 
papers! This added insult to injury. 

A sad letter was received through 
the mail some days later from Esmer¬ 
alda’s ghost. She was not coming back, 
not under any circumstances. Her treat¬ 
ment choked her whenever she thought 
of it. She was leaving for other scenes 
and other climes, and any papers found 
round and about would be the campers’ 
own responsibility, so there! 

Margaret Govan, Gamp Onawaw 


Toronto, Canada, February 1963 


57 




by Margaret Go van s 
Camp Onawaw 


Story telling is becoming a lost art. 
Yet stories belong to children and the 
dividends realized from making use of 
stories are enormous. They are a pain¬ 
less method of teaching humour, imag¬ 
ination, history, religion, ethics, atti¬ 
tudes, understanding, ad infinitum. It 
takes time to tell a story well, and even 
more time to find a story worth telling! 
But you will be repaid a hundredfold 
in the attention and delight of the 
listeners, by the effectiveness of the 
stories in their lives, and by your own 
experiences of creative activity — be¬ 
cause the story teller belongs among 
the artists of this world. 

Where do you find your stories? In 
all sorts of strange places as well as in 
the to-be-expected sources. The Satur¬ 
day Evening Post has provided me with 
many a story for seniors; there are 
many episodes you can choose from 
the classics; try an enlargement on 
your own experiences (children love to 
hear stories about you when you were 
young, even although you may still be 
in your teens!); look into the history 
of your particular locality as well as 
history in general; the story of a play 
(J. M. Barrie has given me many a 
good story —Mary Rose is an excellent 
ghost story). And then there are the 
story collections to be found in every 
public library. 


STORY 

TELLING 

How do you learn them? I read 
the story slowly and carefully, and do 
it several times. I go over the sequence 
of events. I try to see it in my mind, 
like a movie. I try to feel my way 
into it. Often, I write it out. I tell it 
to the bedpost. I take time for the 
preparation of every story that I tell, 
whether it be for the first time of 
telling or the tenth time. 

I keep my listeners in mind and 
would use a different vocabulary and 
also a different slant for younger or for 
older campers. How do you tell the 
stories? As simply as possible. No over- 
dramatization. Unless the humour 
demands it, I don’t use long words that 
cause a block in the movement of the 
story. No very involved plots with sub¬ 
plots. Only a few characters. No re¬ 
capitulations because some event was 
forgotten. And keep yourself out of it 
as much as possible; be inconspicuous; 
be lost in the story along with your 
listeners. 

When do you tell stories? At camp¬ 
fires—at the dining-room table. On 
wet days, on hot days. At parties, with 
the cabin group whenever possible. 
Reading aloud is a good substitute. In 
fact some stories should be memorized 
or read aloud such as the Just So 
Stories, Winnie-the-Pooh, poetry, and 
stories which have a special flavour.

George Williams College 
announces 

Master’s Degree in Camping 


George Williams College,, Chicago, 
lias inaugurated a graduate programme 
in camping and outdoor education this 
fall. The programme will lead toward 
a Master of Science degree. 

In announcing the programme, Dr. 
Richard E. Hamlin, President, said it 
was created “to meet the challenge of 
the increasing importance of outdoor 
recreation education.” 

The college, founded in 1890, special¬ 
izes in professional education for 
careers in health education, physical 
education, community recreation and 
group work. Graduates of the college 
serve in YMCA’s, Boys’ Clubs, schools, 
colleges, youth organizations, public 
recreation programmes and in organ¬ 
ized camp administration. 

“Careers in camping and outdoor 
education,” said Dr. Hamlin, “are 
among the most satisfying that qualified 
men and women can enter. The broad¬ 
ened scope of the organized camping 
field, the current trend toward the em¬ 
ployment of full-time administrators, 
and the increased emphasis on the im¬ 
portance of the qualified director, have 
created a need for educational pro¬ 
gramming and preparation.” 

He said the master’s degree pro¬ 
gramme in camping and outdoor edu¬ 
cation at the college is designed to 
prepare students for careers in organ¬ 
ized camp administration, school¬ 
camping, teaching or nature-recreation 
leadership. Each of these fields is in¬ 
creasing in importance in career oppor¬ 
tunities, he added. 

One-third of the new master’s 
degree programme is related to group 
work, guidance and counselling, group 


dynamics and research. Another third 
is related to administration of outdoor 
education and camping programmes. 
The final third is a nature-recreation 
education sequence, designed specific¬ 
ally for use in informal educational 
programming. 

Candidates for degrees are required 
to complete field work requirements in 
museums, forest preserves and com¬ 
munity centres. This field work involves 
grou p leadership, nature-recreation 
education, camp leadership, and school 
camping programmes. 

George Williams College is fully ac¬ 
credited, coeducational nondemonina- 
tional and is one of the oldest colleges 
in the United States preparing pro¬ 
fessional leaders for youth organizations, 
recreation and camping programmes, 
and schools. It has been recognized as 
one of the pioneering institutions in the 
field of organized camping, and much 
of the field’s literature has been 
authored by the faculty. 

In describing this new programme 
college officials state, “There are two 
definite and unique contributions that 
organized camping offers its partici¬ 
pants: personality, social and character 
growth through the group living ex¬ 
perience, and knowledge and use of 
the out-of-doors. These two areas serve 
as the foundation for the master’s 
curriculum.” 

As well as the degree described here, 
the college offers degrees at both the 
bachelor’s and master’s levels in health 
education, physical education, com¬ 
munity recreation and group work. 


All inquiries concerning this or other 
programmes at the college should be 
directed to: 

Director of Admissions, 

George Williams College, 

5315 South Drexel Avenue, 
Chicago 15, Illinois .

The scheme has come to Canada— 
in experimental form at least. 

Following a visit of His Royal High¬ 
ness in 1962, a group of Canadian 
Youth leaders met about the possi¬ 
bilities of introducing the scheme to 
Canada. To this end the Y.M.C.A. in 
Canada was asked to conduct a trial 
run of the scheme. 

Five associations across Canada were 
selected as centres for the experiment. 
These are the five associations: Halifax. 
Toronto, Vancouver, Chatham, and 
Kitchener-W aterloo. 

In order to conduct this experiment 
in the Kitchener-Waterloo Y.M.C.A. a 
steering committee was formed, with 
representation from various programme 
departments. One such department is 
our camping department which has 
been asked to study the implications of 
the scheme for the camping pro¬ 
gramme, particularly the area connected 
with expeditions. Since the Ontario 
Camping Association has been asked to 
consider its role in connection with the 
scheme experiment in Canada, we are 
presenting this preliminary report for 
the information of the Canadian Camp¬ 
ing movement. 

First Series (Bronze Award) 

Foot expeditions only, one night 
camping out, 15 miles in length in 
normal country. 

1. pre-requisite training in map read¬ 
ing and orientation. 

2. elementary knowledge of personal 
hygiene. 

3. first aid training in proper report¬ 
ing of accidents, and theory and 
practical work to the Junior St. 
John’s Ambulance level. 

4. knowledge of rules and courtesies 
of cross-country travel (i.e. trespass 
laws, fire regulations, etc.) 

5. knowledge of campsite planning 
and organization (e.g. site selection 
and layout, latrine plan, refuse 
disposal, etc.)

Second Series (Silver Award) 

Choice of foot, canoe, sailing, horse¬ 
back, etc., expedition of at least two 
nights out at different sites and 30 
miles in length in normal country. 

1. pre-requisite: successful completion 
of a first series expedition or 
equivalent, and further training in 
map work, compass and campcraft. 

2. same as for first series except 
longer duration and increased 
variety in methods of travel (i.e. 
canoe, horseback, etc.) 

Third Series (Gold Award) 

Expeditions of at least 50 miles in 
length and 3 nights out at different 
sites, in wild country. 

1. pre-requisite: successful completion 
of requirement for first and second 
series or equivalents, and addi¬ 
tional knowledge of first aid. (As 
a precaution, participants should 
have added experience to the ex¬ 
peditions required for the first 
and second series before attempt¬ 
ing the third series.) 

2. same as for second series except 
longer duration and in wild 
country. 

3. knowledge of weather conditions in 
areas chosen for the expedition, 
and ability to recognize weather 
signs. 

4. knowledge of safety precautions re¬ 
quired for travel in the areas 
chosen for the expedition .(i.e. 
knowledge of communications cen¬ 
tres, rescue posts, ranger stations, 
etc.) 

General Requirements for All Series 

1. participants must demonstrate a 
knowledge of clothing and equip¬ 
ment essential to the expedition 
undertaken (e.g. first aid kit, flash¬ 
light, proper packing).

A fifth difference is that there are 
bottles of coke syrup at all strategic 
points in the camp. Our counsellors 
are alerted to be on the lookout for 
reactions, and have been instructed 
in what to do. Many of our counsellors 
themselves are diabetics, and they are 
invaluable in encouraging the campers 
to participate in camp activities. 

Sixthly, there is urine testing just 
prior to every meal and again at bed¬ 
time. There must be testing stations 
with running water where this can be 
done. There must be clinitest, test 
tubes and some responsible person to 
supervise and record the test results. 

Yet, with all these differences, we 
still can maintain a camp-like atmos¬ 
phere and a camp programme. The 
girls sleep in cabins, the boys in tents. 
This summer we had about an equal 
number of French and English speaking 
boys and girls. The campers’ favourite 
indoor activity proved to be dancing 
(mixers, reels, squares and the “twist”), 
While outdoors they loved counsellor 
hunts. The camp is operated by the 
■Quebec Camp for Diabetic Children 
Inc. and is financed by donations from 
interested individuals and local bene¬ 
volent organizations.

A WARBLER'S 
APPETITE 

By F. West ma n 


In 1961 there were many casualties 
among night flying migrants at the 
Barrie, Ontario T.V. tower. On Sep¬ 
tember 13, we found 517 dead birds 
and 23 injured, of 30 species. The 
dead birds were sent to the Royal 
Ontario Museum for research purposes, 
and the injured were taken to Mr. 
Ivor’s bird sanctuary at Erindale. One 
little chestnut-sided warbler with a 
broken wing was left behind by mistake, 
so after a telephone consultation with 
Mr. Ivor, I undertook to set his wing 
and feed him. 

I did not anticipate having to pro¬ 
vide great quantities of food for such 
a tiny creature, but how wrong 1 
proved to be! In the end it took three 
of us most of the day to capture enough 
insects to satisfy his appcite. We started 
off' the morning by giving him four 
moths which looked big enough to do 
him till lunch. At first he was too shy 
to eat while we watched, so we dis¬ 
creetly retired. Ten minutes later no 
moths—just wings. I caught 28 spiders 
and dropped them in the box. They 
were devoured in quick succession as 
we peeked through a crack. Desperately 
searching for more food we came up 
with a green leggy creature, a small 
green caterpillar, and 35 little worms 
discovered in webs in oak leaves. By 
this time the little warbler knew that 
when we opened the lid it meant food, 
and he would grab the offerings and 
down them as we proferred them. After 
partaking of 28 more spiders, a cut¬ 



Reprinted from 
The Federation of 
Ontario Naturalists Bulletin 
with the Editor's kind permission 


worm, three tiny centipedes and two 
small hairy caterpillars, he was still 
looking for food, and we were at our 
wits end! There were a good many 
yellow sulphur butterflies flying about, 
so we tried him with one of these 
(after a wild chase with a butterfly 
net). Off came the wings and “down 
the hatch” went the butterfly’s body, 
so we caught 10 more which all suffered 
the same fate. Next we tried him with 
grasshoppers, which were plentiful and 
comparatively easy to catch. He wasn’t 
too keen on them, but ate five. Another 
spider, a moth, a small hairy caterpillar 
and one more leggy creature were con¬ 
sumed before it mercifully grew dark 
while there was still something left 
of the three large humans who were 
trying to satisfy the appetite of one 
little five-inch warbler! 

The next day was perhaps a little 
easier as we found he liked crickets, 
and we became fairly adept at catching 
them, though it did take time. He ate 
34. The most interesting thing lie ate 
that day was a female stick insect full 
of eggs. He had quite a battle before 
he killed her—she was nearly as long 
as lie, and defended herself bravely. 
We offered him the male stick insect 
also, very thin and dry and hard 
looking. Evidently the warbler thought 
so too, as lie would not touch it. The 
toll for that day was: six grasshoppers.

Canadian Camping 


from page 49 

Possible variations in the ground water 
level should also be kept in mind when 
selecting the site of any sewage dis¬ 
posal system because the ground water 
level fluctuates—from high during the 
wet season to low during the dry 
season. 

The privy should be located from 50 
to 150 feet down-wind from all camp 
buildings, 100 feet from the kitchen, 
and at least 100 feet from a lake or 
stream. 

Additional considerations in the con¬ 
struction of a sanitary earth pit privy 
are adequate ventilation of both the pit 
and the superstructure, and a raised 
impervious floor, with earth mounded 
around the outside of the privy and 
sloping away from it to divert surface 
drainage. Privies especially should be 
made as fly-proof as possible. This in¬ 
cludes filling or screening any knot 
holes in the sides of the structure, 
screening all openings such as windows 
and vents, making the door self-closing 
and providing a self-closing device for 
the seat lid. The lid may be made 
self-closing by the use of spring loaded 
hinges or by the simple application of 
a board or spring behind the seat which 
will not permit the lid to open far 
enough for it to be free-standing. Pro¬ 
vided the privy is kept clean and the 
contents are covered with dry earth or 
a commercial preparation, few prob¬ 
lems will be encountered. Waste water 
and surface drainage should not be 
allowed to enter the pit, but if water 
does gain entrance, a small amount of 
kerosene or fuel oil will prevent the 
breeding of mosquitos. 

Where an earth privy cannot be used 
because of high water table or insuf¬ 
ficient depth of soil in which to dig 
the pit, a pail type or concrete vault 
type of privy may be used. 

The pail type privy is a temporary 
installation which can be used provided 


a suitable site for the disposal of the 
contents of the pails is available. The 
contents may be disposed of in an 
excreta pit, which is a covered pit with 
open jointed walls in porous ground or 
coarse gravel or stone which will per¬ 
mit the liquid to leach away without 
contaminating the ground water. The 
disposal pit should have an open bot¬ 
tom which is at least two and prefer¬ 
ably four feet above the highest eleva¬ 
tion of the ground water table. In 
general the maintenance problems asso¬ 
ciated with pail privies such as the 
difficulties in handling and emptying 
the pails and the control of odour 
render them useful only when no other 
means are available. 

The concrete vault privy is equipped 
with a water-tight concrete vault for 
the excreta. This is emptied through 
an opening with a hinged cover located 
at the back of the privy. This cover 
frequently becomes warped and thus no 
longer fly-proof. The same problem of 
handling and disposal associated with 
pail privies makes them unsuitable ex¬ 
cept in the most extreme circumstances. 

Where soil conditions are such that 
sewage cannot be disposed of by privies 
or septic tank systems, it follows that 
there must be a treated effluent which 
must be discharged eventually to a 
watercourse or a lake. In any such 
installation, the agency responsible for 
stream pollution control should be con¬ 
sulted. In some cases, the use of a 
sewage lagoon has resulted in succesful 
treatment of sewage in a summer camp 
where the more common methods of 
treatment are not possible. CAN¬ 
ADIAN CAMPING, December 1961 
issue, page 24 contains an excellent 
article on sewage lagoons for those 
interested in this type of system. 

To recapitulate, the essential points 
to remember in the installation of any 
sewage disposal system are that it be so 
constructed that it will not:

(1) Permit sewage to lie exposed on 
the ground where it will be 
accessible to children, pets, rodents 
or insects. 

(2) Contaminate a drinking water 
supply. 

(3) Pollute any bathing water, fishing 
ground or surface water used for 
recreational purposes. 

(4) Create any nuisance or unsightly 
condition. 

The methods that have been men¬ 
tioned—the various types of privies, the 
septic tank and tile bed or modified 
water carriage systems—will, if properly 
installed, ensure that none of the above 
mentioned unsatisfactory conditions will 
prevail. 

In nearly all provinces, expert advice 
can be obtained from local or provin¬ 
cial health authorities. Some jurisdic¬ 
tion require that permission be obtained 
before disposal systems are installed. In 
Ontario, for example, the local Medical 
Officer of Health must approve any 
subsurface sewage disposal system be¬ 
fore its installation. 

Many provinces also distribute book¬ 
lets which a camp operator will find of 
great interest and benefit. Copies of 
Ontario’s booklet may be obtained on 
request from the Environmental Sani¬ 
tation Branch, 67 College Street, 
Toronto 2, Ontario. 

It is hoped that the foregoing re¬ 
marks will be of benefit to those 
charged with the satisfactory operation 
of a summer camp. It should be appre¬ 
ciated that the remarks are, of necessity, 
general in nature. It is expected that, 
where a large installation is required or 
difficult terrain is encountered, the ser¬ 
vices of a professional sanitary engineer 
experienced in this field will be ob¬ 
tained. A properly designed and in¬ 
stalled system will require relatively 
little maintenance and thus add to the 
camping enjoyment of all concerned.

from page 45 

architect of his future.” Perhaps in our 
desire to be more democratic, to create 
mental giants, and in our eagerness to 
please, we have watered down the im¬ 
portant values which build strong char¬ 
acter and responsible citizenship. Char¬ 
acter is the distinguishing mark, 
signifying what our training, habits and 
thoughts have made us. Mind without 
heart, intelligence without conduct, 
cleverness without goodness—all have 
dangerous flaws. 

Character, as Goethe tells us, grows 
only in the stream of the world. The tent 
pegs of a good camp programme which 
hold the framework for building good 
character and a sense of responsibility 
are such things as the opportunity to 
make decisions, to help plan, to live 
comfortably in the camping community, 
to appreciate simplicity, to recognize 
the worth of personality, to establish a 
relationship with God, to know' the 
heritage that makes it a privilege to be 
a Canadian, to discipline oneself, to 
learn by doing. We cannot build char¬ 
acter by storing our abilities and virtues 
within ourselves. As Fred Rogers, Past 
President of The American Camping 
Association has pointed out, the chal¬ 
lenge to us today is to stay with the 
job searching for better ways of ac¬ 
complishing it, creating the situation 
and leadership to cause its growth. A 
bold and strong approach, dedicated 
to the principle of influencing for strong 
character among the youth we serve, 
can be our answer to the materialism 
sweeping through our society today. 

In a recent article in the American 
Camping Magazine, under a heading 
“What are the Distinctive Contributions 
of Organized Camping in a Changing 
Society”, one of the contributions listed 
was called spiritual potential. Here in 
part is what was said: “Children have 
a sense of awe and wonder, a feeling 
for purpose and order in the universe, 


a capacity, therefore, for spiritual sensi¬ 
tivity. A child can become sensitive to 
a deep wisdom not gained from books. 
This quality too often withers and dies 
. . . because of the insensitivity and 
the cheap cynicism of adults. The most 
precious of things spiritual, should be 
fostered in every possible way at camp. 
And everything that happens at camp 
can have spiritual overtones. This 
spiritual awareness, once stimulated, 
may carry over into the home and into 
life in general.” 

“One of the worst effects of urban 
living is the increasing fear of being 
alone. A person who has discovered 
the rich inner resources of his being 
welcomes opportunities for aloneness. 
At camp he can gain an appreciation 
of solitude if the day provides for 
opportunities to be alone. There will 
be chances to read, to enjoy a sunset, 
to study nature’s forms and colours, 
perhaps to try to create them in sketch 
or painting or in some other art form.” 

We camp leaders may know what we 
should be trying to do, but we can 
stumble over the how of the doing. 
This how-of-doing must be related to 
you, the director or the staff member, as 
a person. The things you believe you 
will easily express in action and words. 
Do the things that are natural and 
meaningful to you, and they will be 
meaningful to your staff and campers 
also. Even if your thoughts are simply 
expressed, children can sense your sin¬ 
cerity, and your conviction will mean 
something to them. Be simple and be 
sincere. 

Then, too, you cannot draw water 
from a dry well. If you are going to 
give leadership in any area you must 
have some knowledge of the area before 
you can .lead. You will need to re¬ 
plenish and add to your knowledge 
about things spiritual. By reading, by 
securing good resource material, by 


68 


Canadian Camping 


having a sound philosophy of life, by 
relating what you read and feel and 
think to what you do and say. This 
is not easy, but that it can be even 
partially accomplished is evidenced by 
the letters from parents or the intima¬ 
tions by campers themselves of what 
camp has meant to them. 

With these efforts our convictions 
deepen that camping has a more last¬ 
ing value than “skills” alone—it has 
at its heart as a beautiful core, the art 
of learning how to live, to put down 
roots in a stable soil within this transi¬ 
tory, mobile world. To transmit to our 
campers this sense of values, a sense of 
belonging, a sense of stability—this is 
perhaps the greatest challenge of camp¬ 
ing today. 

Let me conclude with a camper’s 
poem which expresses so well what I 
have been trying to say: 

God is my friend, 

I met Him long ago 
I cannot quite remember where. 

At first I did not know Him well 
Although I spoke to Him each day 
And sang to Him each Sunday. 

The words were copied from a book, 
And He seemed far away. 

Then came a summer and I went 
to camp. 

Each night we climbed a hill 
To sit and talk with God; 

Not for the usual drowsy minute 
before bedtime, 

But a long, thinking silence. 

The sunset sky, the curving hills, the 
grass and trees 

Opened my heart a little wider than 
before 

In thankfulness for beauty 
everywhere. 

And through the opening came God, 
Not rushing in, but moving quietly 
To talk with me. 


from page 64 

12 spiders, one female walking stick 
with eggs, 43 oak worms, 34 crickets, 
two sulphur butterflies, one bee-like fly, 
two caterpillars, two small centipedes. 

This experience really brought home 
to me the tremendous usefulness of the 
warblers alone in controlling insects. 
This family, the second largest bird 
family in North America, is almost 
entirely insectivorous. To multiply the 
number of insects eaten by the number 
of warblers would, of course produce 
astronomical figures, provided anyone 
knew how many warblers there are. 
But think of it in reverse, and imagine 
if there were wo warblers how many 
insects there would be. Some other 
method of keeping down their numbers 
would have to be quickly found, or 
life on earth would soon be destroyed. 
So such a beautiful little creature as a 
warbler is seen to have an extremely 
practical value in the scheme of nature. 
Let us all work to keep warblers, and 
all the birds, in their place in that 
scheme. Even if we were able, as some 
contend, to come up with something 
which could control insects as effectively 
as birds do, it is very unlikely that 
whatever it was would have one tenth 
of the charm of even one small 
chestnut-sided warbler.

for so many others, and which has 
brought true happiness and greater 
understanding to all those who have 
been privileged to have had contact 
with him. And beside him stands 
Catherine, his wife and partner, the 
other half of a combination which 
through their quiet wisdom, sincerity of 
purpose, and breadth of thought, have 
made them a living example of what 
today can be termed as success, integ¬ 
rity and, above all, contentment in this 
life.

front page 58 

Reading aloud is a wonderful way to 
settle a cabin group at night, only be 
sure that the book is worth reading, 
and that it is not going to start any 
nightmares. Most of the rules for story 
telling apply here too. 

The following I have tried: 

A good collection of fairy stories. 
Indian stories and legends. 

Animal stories, especially about 
horses. 

Greek myths. 

Bible stories. 

King Arthur’s Knights, and Robin 
Hood as retold by Howard Pyle 
Tajar Tales. 

Uncles Remus. 

Paul Bunyan. 

Missionary and Explorer stories. 
Marlin Pippin in the Apple 
Orchard—Eleanor Fargeon 
(for girls) 

The Jungle Books, and parts of 
Kim—Rudyard Kipling. 

Some of Paul Gallico’s stories. 
Geordie, and Sandy Was a 
Soldier’s Boy—David Walker. 

Rooks for reading aloud : 

The Crock of Gold 
James Stephens. 

The fairy stories of George 
MacDonald. 

Mary Poppins—P. L. Travel's. 
Stuart Little, and Charlotte’s Web 
—Elwyn B. White. 

Green willow—Chute (for senior 
girls). 

1 am looking forward to reading 
campers The Incredible Journey — 
Sheila Burnford (heroes are two dogs 
and a Siamese cat). You might take 
along favourite books from your child¬ 
hood to read. Do see to it that today’s 
campers hear stories—there are hund¬ 
reds that are worth while. Ask your 
Librarian to help you.

Another great 
World Tour in 1963— 
and you can be 
aboard when we sail! 

Now r you can travel completely around the 
world with' a group who will share your 
interests and fun — people you’ll really like. 
You’ll share the excitement of traveling on 
a fine cruise ship, reserved deluxe buses, 
modern jet planes. You’ll visit with other 
youth workers in foreign lands, see important 
people and places on five continents. Best of 
all, you can do this at a price far, far below 
the usual charge for a tour this extensive. 
(Minimum tour cost just $1,475.) 

You can sail in early October from Canada’s 
West Coast and, as you enjoy the sunny days 
at sea. look forward to Honolulu, the Fiji’s, 
Australia, Ceylon. Aden and many other won¬ 
derful lands. When you arrive in Europe, 
your own bus and courier will be waiting to 
take you through the beautiful countryside 
to many famous cities. In December, your 
final adventure will be a jet flight across the 
Atlantic to New York. 

Your place on the 1963 Round-the-World tour 
is waiting. It can be the trip you’ve dreamed 
of — fun, new friends, time to sightsee and 
learn, to rest and to play.
